title: Master Data I — Business Partner (Supplier)
intro: In S/4HANA every supplier is a Business Partner. This module covers how a supplier is structured, which data lives at which level, and how to create, change and block one.
objectives: Explain why S/4HANA uses the Business Partner for suppliers
Distinguish BP categories, roles and groupings
Identify which data is held at general, company code and purchasing organisation level
Create, change and block a supplier with transaction BP

lessons.title: Why the Business Partner?
lessons.body:
In SAP ECC, suppliers (called vendors) and customers had separate master records and transactions (XK01, FK01, MK01…). In S/4HANA, the Business Partner (BP) is the single entry point for both.

  • Transaction BP replaces the old vendor transactions, which now redirect to BP
  • One BP can be both a supplier and a customer, sharing one name and address
  • Customer-Vendor Integration (CVI) runs in the background and keeps the classic supplier tables in sync, so older reports and processes still work

BP category: what kind of partner?

  • Person: an individual
  • Organisation: a company (most suppliers)
  • Group: e.g. a married couple or joint venture

The category is chosen at creation and can't be changed afterwards.

BP role: what does the partner do for us?

Roles add data views. For suppliers, three matter:

RoleNameAdds
000000Business Partner (General)Name, address, communication, bank, tax
FLVN00FI SupplierCompany code data (accounting)
FLVN01SupplierPurchasing organisation data

BP grouping

The grouping controls the number range (internal or external numbering) and, through CVI, the supplier account group. Typical groupings: domestic suppliers, foreign suppliers, one-time suppliers, employees.

Learners coming from ECC often look for XK01. Show them it redirects to BP in the first five minutes, and the resistance drops.
lessons.narration: In the old SAP system, ECC, suppliers were called vendors, and they had their own master records and transactions, completely separate from customers. In S/4HANA, that changed. Every supplier and every customer is now a Business Partner, maintained with one transaction: B P. The old vendor transactions still exist, but they simply redirect you to B P. One business partner can even be a supplier and a customer at the same time, sharing a single name and address. Behind the scenes, something called Customer-Vendor Integration keeps the classic supplier tables in sync, so older reports keep working. When you create a business partner, you first choose a category. Person, for an individual. Organisation, for a company, which is what most suppliers are. Or group. Be careful: the category can't be changed later. Next, you add roles. Each role adds a set of data. For suppliers, three roles matter. The general role, zero zero zero zero zero zero, holds the name, address, bank and tax details. The role F L V N zero zero, F I Supplier, adds the accounting data for a company code. And the role F L V N zero one, Supplier, adds the purchasing data for a purchasing organisation. Finally, the grouping decides the number range, meaning whether the system assigns the number or you enter it yourself. A practical tip for class: learners coming from the old system always look for X K zero one. Show them early that it redirects to B P, and the resistance disappears.
keyTerms: Single master record for suppliers and customers in S/4HANA
Customer-Vendor Integration: syncs BP with classic supplier/customer tables
Person, Organisation or Group; cannot be changed later
Adds a data view, e.g. FLVN00 (FI Supplier), FLVN01 (Supplier)
Controls number range and maps to the supplier account group

tryIt.task: Type XK03 in SAP GUI and observe what happens.
Open BP, display an existing supplier and use the 'Display in BP role' dropdown to switch between 000000, FLVN00 and FLVN01. Note what changes on screen.

lessons.title: General data
lessons.body:
General data is shared across the whole client: every company code and purchasing organisation sees the same values.

Main tabs (role 000000)

  • Address: name, search terms, street, postcode, city, country, language, communication (phone, email)
  • Address overview: additional addresses, e.g. a separate ordering or remittance address
  • Identification: tax numbers (e.g. VAT registration number), industry, legal form
  • Control: e.g. authorisation group, customer link
  • Payment transactions: bank details (country, bank key, account / IBAN)
  • Status: central blocks, archiving flag

Why it matters

  • The address and language decide what prints on purchase orders sent to the supplier
  • Search terms are what users type to find the supplier, so agree a naming convention
  • Bank details are used by the payment run in FI, which makes them sensitive. Many companies use dual control (one person changes, another approves)

Duplicate suppliers are the most common master data problem in real companies. Always search before you create.
lessons.narration: General data is shared across the whole client. Every company code and every purchasing organisation sees exactly the same values. In the general role, you'll find several tabs. Address holds the name, search terms, street, city, country, language and contact details. Address overview lets you add extra addresses, for example a separate ordering address. Identification holds tax numbers, such as the VAT registration number, plus industry and legal form. Payment transactions holds bank details, the bank country, bank key and account number or IBAN. And Status is where central blocks live. Why does this matter? The address and the language decide what appears on purchase orders sent to the supplier. Search terms are what users type to find the supplier, so it's worth agreeing a naming convention. And bank details feed the payment run in finance, so they're sensitive. Many companies insist on dual control, where one person changes bank details and another approves them. One last point to stress with learners: duplicate suppliers are the most common master data problem in real companies. Always search before you create.
keyTerms: Client-wide supplier data shared by all company codes and purchasing orgs
Short text used to find the BP quickly
International bank account number, stored in Payment transactions
Sensitive changes (e.g. bank details) need confirmation by a second user

tryIt.task: Search for suppliers with BP using a search term or city. Try the wildcard *, e.g. *PARIS*.
Display one supplier's Address, Identification and Payment transactions tabs and note what is filled in.

lessons.title: Company code data (FI Supplier)
lessons.body:
Role FLVN00 adds data per company code. A supplier used by two legal entities has two sets of company code data.

Key fields

  • Reconciliation account (mandatory): the G/L account in FI that collects all postings to this supplier, typically Accounts Payable – domestic or foreign
  • Sort key: controls the default assignment field on line items
  • Payment terms: used for invoices posted in FI
  • Payment methods: e.g. bank transfer, cheque
  • Check double invoice: warns if the same invoice is posted twice
  • Posting block / payment block

Why MM people need to know this

When an invoice is posted in MIRO, the amount payable goes to the supplier account in this company code, and FI picks it up via the reconciliation account. Without FLVN00 data for the company code, the invoice can't be posted.

Payment terms exist in both company code data and purchasing data. The PO normally takes them from the purchasing data, and the invoice takes them from the PO.
lessons.narration: The role F L V N zero zero, F I Supplier, adds data per company code. If two legal entities buy from the same supplier, there are two sets of company code data. The most important field is the reconciliation account, and it's mandatory. It's the general ledger account in finance that collects every posting to this supplier, usually accounts payable, domestic or foreign. You'll also find the sort key, payment terms, payment methods such as bank transfer, the check for double invoices, and posting and payment blocks. Why should MM people care about accounting data? Because when someone posts a supplier invoice in M I R O, the amount payable goes to this supplier's account in this company code. If the company code data doesn't exist, the invoice simply can't be posted. One subtle point: payment terms exist both here and in the purchasing data. The purchase order normally takes them from the purchasing data, and the invoice then takes them from the purchase order.
keyTerms: FI Supplier role: company code (accounting) data
G/L account collecting all postings for the supplier; mandatory
Rules for due date and cash discount
Warns when the same invoice is entered twice

tryIt.task: Display a supplier in role FLVN00 using the 'Company Code' button. Find the reconciliation account and payment terms.
Check whether the same supplier has data in more than one company code.

lessons.title: Purchasing data and partner functions
lessons.body:
Role FLVN01 adds data per purchasing organisation. Without it, you can't create a PO for this supplier in that purchasing org.

Key purchasing fields

  • Order currency
  • Payment terms and Incoterms (e.g. EXW, DAP, DDP): copied into the PO
  • Minimum order value
  • Schema group: determines which pricing procedure is used (Module 8)
  • GR-based invoice verification: invoices can only be matched to goods already received (Module 7)
  • Order acknowledgement required
  • Automatic purchase order: allows requisitions to be converted to POs automatically
  • Purchasing group and planned delivery time (defaults)

Partner functions

A supplier can play different roles in one transaction. Partner functions link them:

CodeFunctionExample
VNSupplier (vendor)The main supplier
OAOrdering addressWhere the PO is sent
GSGoods supplierWho actually ships
PIInvoicing partyWho sends the invoice and gets paid

By default all four point to the supplier itself. You change them when, for example, a head office invoices but a regional depot delivers.

Most PO defaults come from here. When a learner asks “where did this currency or these payment terms come from?”, the answer is almost always the purchasing data.
lessons.narration: The role F L V N zero one, Supplier, adds data per purchasing organisation. Without it, you can't create a purchase order for this supplier in that purchasing organisation. The key fields are: order currency; payment terms and Incoterms, such as ex works or delivered duty paid, which are copied into the purchase order; minimum order value; the schema group, which decides the pricing procedure, and we'll see that in module eight; G R based invoice verification, which means invoices can only be matched against goods already received; order acknowledgement required; and automatic purchase order, which allows requisitions to be turned into orders automatically. Then there are partner functions. In a single transaction, different companies can play different parts. V N is the supplier itself. O A is the ordering address, where the purchase order is sent. G S is the goods supplier, who actually ships. And P I is the invoicing party, who sends the invoice and gets paid. By default, all four point to the same supplier. You change them when, say, a head office invoices but a regional depot delivers. Here's the trainer takeaway: most defaults on a purchase order come from the purchasing data. When a learner asks where a currency or payment term came from, that's almost always the answer.
keyTerms: International delivery terms, e.g. EXW, DAP, DDP
Invoice can only be matched to quantities already received
Supplier setting that helps determine the pricing procedure
VN supplier, OA ordering address, GS goods supplier, PI invoicing party

tryIt.task: Display a supplier in role FLVN01 using the 'Purchasing' button. Note the order currency, payment terms, Incoterms and GR-based IV flag.
Open the Partner Functions tab and check which partners are assigned.
Open an existing PO for that supplier (ME23N) and compare its currency, payment terms and Incoterms with the purchasing data.

lessons.title: One-time suppliers, blocking and changes
lessons.body:
One-time suppliers

  • For suppliers you rarely use, creating a full master record is wasteful
  • A one-time supplier record (special grouping) is a generic account: the name, address and bank details are entered in each document instead

Blocking a supplier

BlockEffect
Purchasing block (purchasing org level)No new POs in that purchasing org
Posting block (company code)No FI postings, e.g. invoices
Payment blockInvoices can be posted but not paid
Central blockBlocks across all organisational levels

Suppliers are rarely deleted. They're blocked first, then marked for deletion and archived later.

Tracking changes

  • All changes are logged: in BP use Extras → Change history (menu names vary slightly by release)
  • Sensitive fields such as bank details can require dual control

Full exercise: create a supplier end-to-end

  1. BP → Create Organisation → choose the domestic supplier grouping
  2. Role 000000: name, search term, address, language, VAT number, bank details
  3. Switch to role FLVN00 → Company Code → enter your company code, reconciliation account, payment terms
  4. Switch to role FLVN01 → Purchasing → enter your purchasing org, order currency, payment terms, Incoterms, GR-based IV
  5. Save, note the BP number, then create a test PO for it in ME21N

This exercise is your best classroom activity for this module. Learners see straight away which missing data blocks the PO.
lessons.narration: Let's finish with special cases. For suppliers you'll only use once or twice, creating a full master record is wasteful. Instead, you use a one-time supplier. It's a generic account, and the actual name, address and bank details are typed into each document instead. Next, blocking. There are several kinds of block. A purchasing block, at purchasing organisation level, stops new purchase orders. A posting block, at company code level, stops accounting postings such as invoices. A payment block lets invoices be posted, but not paid. And a central block blocks the supplier everywhere. In practice, suppliers are almost never deleted straight away. They're blocked first, then marked for deletion, and archived later. All changes to a business partner are logged, and you can view them through the change history. Sensitive fields such as bank details can be protected with dual control. Now it's your turn. In the system, create a complete supplier: the general data, then company code data in role F L V N zero zero, then purchasing data in role F L V N zero one. Save it, note the number, and create a test purchase order for it. In class, this is the best exercise for the module, because learners immediately see which missing data blocks the purchase order.
keyTerms: Generic BP; address and bank entered in each document
Prevents new purchasing documents for the supplier
Prevents accounting postings in a company code
Invoices can be posted but not paid
Marks a supplier for later archiving

tryIt.task: Do the full exercise above: create a supplier with all three roles, then create a test PO for it in ME21N.
Set a purchasing block on your new supplier, try to create another PO, note the message, then remove the block.
Trainer kit: write a one-page job aid 'Creating a supplier in BP' with screenshots of each step.

quiz.q: In S/4HANA, which transaction is used to create a supplier?
quiz.explain: BP is the single transaction for business partners. The old vendor transactions redirect to it.

quiz.q: Which BP role holds purchasing organisation data?
quiz.explain: FLVN01 (Supplier) holds purchasing data. FLVN00 holds company code data; FLCU01 is a customer role.

quiz.q: Which field is mandatory in the supplier's company code data?
quiz.explain: The reconciliation account links the supplier to the general ledger and is required.

quiz.q: What does the BP grouping control?
quiz.explain: The grouping determines internal or external numbering and maps to the supplier account group.

quiz.q: A head office sends invoices but a depot ships the goods. Which partner functions differ?
quiz.explain: PI (invoicing party) is the head office; GS (goods supplier) is the depot.

quiz.q: Where does a new PO normally take its order currency from?
options: Purchasing org data of the supplier
quiz.explain: Order currency, payment terms and Incoterms default from the supplier's purchasing data.

quiz.q: Which statement about the BP category is true?
options: It can be changed at any time
It cannot be changed after creation
It is only used for customers
quiz.explain: Person, Organisation or Group is fixed once the BP is created.

quiz.q: A supplier should still receive POs but must not be paid for now. Which block?
quiz.explain: A payment block allows invoices to be posted but stops payment.

quiz.q: Why might an invoice fail to post for a supplier that exists in BP?
options: No FLVN00 data for that company code
quiz.explain: Invoice posting needs the supplier's company code data, including the reconciliation account.

quiz.q: When is a one-time supplier appropriate?
options: For your main raw material supplier
For a supplier used very rarely
quiz.explain: One-time suppliers avoid creating full master records for rarely used suppliers.

howToTeach: Start with a quick 'why BP' story: one partner, many roles
Draw three layers on the board: general → company code → purchasing org, then map each tab to a layer
Use the end-to-end creation exercise; let learners hit the error when a role is missing
commonMistakes: Forgetting to switch roles, so company code or purchasing data is never created
Creating duplicates instead of searching first
Editing bank details without following the company's dual-control process
Confusing payment terms in company code data with those in purchasing data
demoScript: Run XK03 to show the redirect to BP
Search for an existing supplier and walk through roles 000000, FLVN00 and FLVN01
Create a new supplier live with all three roles
Create a PO in ME21N and show the defaults coming from FLVN01
Set and remove a purchasing block
